title: How the error is computed: expectation, outcome, and subtraction

html:
The preceding section established what the basal ganglia’s error signal represents–a scalar (or population-level) temporal-difference prediction error δ=r+γV(s′)−V(s)\delta=r+\gamma V(s')−V(s)–and what loss landscape it serves. This section asks the circuit-level question: how is that error actually computed? In the most stripped-down form, computing δ requires three quantities to be available at the right time and combined with the right arithmetic: (i) an expectation signal, V(s), representing the predicted value of the current state; (ii) an outcome signal, representing the reward actually received together with the discounted value of the successor state, r+γV(s′)r+\gamma V(s'); and (iii) a subtraction operation that takes the difference between the two. These three ingredients must converge on the dopamine neuron at the moment an outcome occurs or a prediction is updated, yielding the signed error whose broadcast to striatum drives the plasticity described in subsequent sections. A 2025 preprint tests a striatal–dopamine learning circuit (Figure) 18.

To understand how the midbrain implements this comparison, it is essential to appreciate the input architecture of VTA and SNc dopamine neurons. Whole-brain mapping of direct (monosynaptic) inputs to dopamine neurons reveals an extraordinarily broad afferent landscape: dopamine neurons receive convergent projections from the ventral and dorsal striatum, ventral pallidum, lateral hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus, lateral habenula, rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg), pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg), dorsal raphe, prefrontal cortex, and other structures 1, 2. Each of these inputs can, in principle, convey some component of the information needed for the RPE computation–actual reward, predicted reward, or some mixture of the two. The critical organizing question is which of these afferents carries the expectation term, which carries the outcome term, and how they are combined at the level of the dopamine neuron to yield a subtracted error. The preprint records striatal projection neurons (Figure).

A landmark result on the arithmetic of the computation came from Eshel, Bukwich, Rao, and colleagues, who combined optogenetic manipulations with extracellular recordings in the VTA during classical conditioning. By delivering rewards of varying magnitudes that were either temporally unexpected or temporally expected (preceded by an odour cue), they were able to ask a precise question: does temporal expectation suppress dopamine reward responses in a subtractive or divisive fashion? If the operation is division, then the expectation-induced reduction should be proportionally larger for larger reward responses; if it is subtraction, the reduction should be a constant offset regardless of reward size. Light-identified dopamine neurons showed a purely subtractive shift: the dose-response curve for reward responses was displaced downward by a constant amount when reward was expected, with no change in slope 3. This is exactly the operation required by the TD error equation δ=r+γV(s′)−V(s)\delta=r+\gamma V(s')−V(s), in which the predicted value is subtracted from the obtained outcome. Subtraction, though intuitively simple, is rarely observed at the single-cell level in the brain–most forms of inhibitory gain modulation produce divisive rather than subtractive effects–making the dopamine neuron’s implementation noteworthy and important for the fidelity of RL 3. The preprint tests effects of striatal stimulation (Figure).

Having established that the operation is subtractive, the next question is: which input supplies the expectation term that is subtracted from the reward response? A convergent body of evidence identifies GABA neurons local to the VTA as a major source of this signal. Cohen, Haesler, and colleagues used optogenetic tagging to identify VTA GABA neurons during Pavlovian conditioning, and found that these neurons show sustained, ramping activity that increases between cue onset and the expected time of reward delivery, with the magnitude of this sustained activity varying with the probability and size of the predicted reward–precisely the profile expected of a reward-expectation signal 4. Eshel and colleagues then confirmed the causal role of VTA GABA neurons in the subtraction operation through a complementary pair of manipulations. Optogenetically exciting VTA GABA neurons at the time of reward delivery mimicked the effect of temporal expectation: dopamine reward responses were suppressed in a subtractive fashion, shifting the dose-response curve downward by a constant amount, reproducing the effect of a naturally learned expectation 3. Conversely, optogenetically inhibiting VTA GABA neurons around the time of expected reward partially reversed expectation-dependent suppression, causing dopamine neurons to respond as though reward was more unexpected than it actually was 3. Furthermore, bilateral stimulation of VTA GABA neurons paired with a conditioned odour dramatically reduced anticipatory licking, consistent with an important role for these neurons in the reinforcement-learning loop 3. Together, these results establish a local circuit mechanism: VTA GABA interneurons receive information about predicted reward (from cortical, striatal, and pallidal afferents), produce sustained inhibitory activity proportional to the expectation, and synapse directly onto neighbouring dopamine neurons, where this inhibition implements the subtractive component of the TD error 2, 3. The preprint manipulates a candidate expectation pathway (Figure).

A second major pathway by which the expectation term reaches dopamine neurons involves the lateral habenula (LHb) and the rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg). The LHb is well positioned to represent worse-than-expected outcomes because it sits downstream of an anti-reward forebrain stream, receiving strong input from pallidal structures—especially the GPi/entopeduncular complex–that themselves encode reward omission, non-reward, and aversive contingencies 5, 6. Importantly, this pallido-habenular pathway is not a simple inhibitory BG output; it includes excitatory glutamatergic signaling (and in some cases mixed transmitter phenotypes), allowing the LHb to be driven when outcomes are worse than predicted and suppressed when outcomes are better than predicted 6, 7. The LHb also receives broader hypothalamic and limbic inputs, enabling it to integrate learned reward expectations with internal-state and aversive information into a unified negative evaluative signal. Its influence on dopamine neurons is powerfully inhibitory despite its own projections being glutamatergic, a paradox resolved by the discovery of the RMTg–a GABAergic nucleus positioned between the LHb and the VTA/SNc that converts LHb excitation into dopamine inhibition 8, 9. Ultrastructural evidence confirms a disynaptic pathway: LHb glutamatergic axons synapse onto GABA neurons in the RMTg, which in turn form inhibitory synapses preferentially onto dopamine neurons in the VTA 10. This LHb->RMTg->dopamine pathway is especially important for the negative component of the TD error—the pause in dopamine firing that occurs when an expected reward is omitted. Habenula lesion experiments dissociate this function from the general RPE computation: after habenula lesions, dopamine neurons retain their ability to signal positive prediction errors (bursts to unexpected reward, transfer of responses to reward-predictive cues), but their response to reward omission is greatly attenuated, indicating that the LHb–RMTg system has a uniquely important role in conveying the signal for worse-than-expected outcomes 11. In intact animals, LHb neuron activation precedes the inhibition of dopamine neuron firing at a latency consistent with a disynaptic relay, and stimulation of the LHb inhibits virtually all midbrain dopamine neurons at short latency 5, 12.

If the subtraction is implemented by local VTA GABA neurons and the LHb–RMTg system, what supplies the outcome signal–the excitatory drive that represents r+γV(s′)r+\gamma V(s') at the time of reward (or at the time of a reward-predictive cue)? Several afferent systems are positioned to contribute this term, and they do so because each sits downstream of circuitry that already integrates biologically relevant outcomes, learned reward contingencies, and action-relevant motivational state. The pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg) is especially well placed to provide a fast reward-related drive: embedded within the mesopontine locomotor/arousal system and tightly linked to basal-ganglia output, it carries both state-updating salience signals and learned reward information, with separable neuronal populations encoding sustained predicted reward from cue onset to reward delivery and phasic actual reward at outcome time 13, 2. The lateral hypothalamus contributes a more physiologically grounded signal. Because it has privileged access to feeding, thirst, arousal, and other homeostatic variables, LH can convey not merely whether an event is externally rewarding, but how valuable it is given the organism’s current internal state; correspondingly, LH projections to dopamine neurons are heterogeneous, with some populations relaying appetitive and reward-predictive information and others carrying aversive or defensive signals 1, 2. The ventral pallidum (VP), meanwhile, acts less like a simple relay and more like a convergent valuation hub: receiving dense input from nucleus accumbens and related mesolimbic structures, it integrates cue value, incentive salience, preference, and action-invigoration variables into a downstream estimate of motivational significance 14. Thus, PPTg, LH, and VP come to signal "reward" not because any is a dedicated reward wire, but because each occupies a different point in the transformation from raw outcome to subjective utility: PPTg emphasizes fast outcome- and cue-related reward information, LH grounds value in bodily need and internal state, and VP integrates learned motivational value into a format suitable for action selection. Their convergent excitatory drive therefore supplies much of the r+γV(s′)r+\gamma V(s')-like signal that, after subtraction by inhibitory expectation pathways, yields the signed TD error.

An important insight from recent work, however, is that the RPE computation does not arise from a simple, modular "one input for reward, one input for expectation" architecture. Tian, Huang, Cohen, and colleagues combined rabies-virus-mediated trans-synaptic tracing with optogenetic identification to record from the monosynaptic inputs of dopamine neurons across seven brain areas during classical conditioning. If the textbook modular view were correct, distinct populations of presynaptic neurons should encode pure reward signals or pure expectation signals, and dopamine neurons should combine them. Instead, they found that the information required for RPE computation–actual reward, predicted reward, and mixtures of the two–was distributed and already mixed in monosynaptic input neurons across all brain areas examined, including the striatum, ventral pallidum, lateral hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus, RMTg, and PPTg 14. Only ∼5% of input neurons signaled actual reward in a pure fashion, and only ∼13% signaled expectation purely; the majority of task-responsive input neurons encoded mixtures of reward and expectation, and a substantial fraction (∼18%) already showed aspects of RPE coding—expectation-dependent suppression of reward responses—before these signals even reached dopamine neurons 14. Strikingly, even when the weights assigned to individual input neurons were randomly shuffled, a linear combination of input-neuron activity still approximated the shape of the dopamine RPE, indicating that the activity profiles of monosynaptic inputs are "pre-formatted" such that the downstream dopamine neuron can robustly converge on the correct RPE signal without exquisitely precise synaptic tuning 14. The preprint compares striatal subregions (Figure).

Despite this redundancy and distribution, the contribution of different input structures is not entirely interchangeable. The LHb-RMTg pathway, as noted above, appears to have a relatively unique role in signaling reward omission 11. Among identified monosynaptic inputs, the RMTg is distinctive in that its neurons preferentially show negative reward coding (excited by aversive cues, inhibited by reward cues), whereas monosynaptic inputs from most other areas are predominantly excited by reward-predictive stimuli 14, 8. Similarly, VTA GABA neurons are enriched for sustained expectation-like activity 4, and the PPTg for both tonic predicted-value and phasic actual-reward signals 13. Thus, while the overall computation is distributed and redundant, individual input channels are biased toward particular computational roles–some more excitatory and reward-signaling, others more inhibitory and expectation-signaling–and the dopamine neuron integrates these heterogeneous inputs to construct a more complete RPE than any single input carries on its own.

The picture that emerges, then, is of a multi-layered, convergent subtraction rather than a clean two-input comparator. The dopamine neuron sits at the apex of a network in which multiple excitatory and inhibitory afferents carry overlapping, partially pre-computed error signals. At the most local level, VTA GABA interneurons provide a subtractive expectation signal that suppresses reward responses in proportion to predicted value 3. In parallel, the LHb-RMTg system provides a disynaptic inhibitory pathway that is especially important for signaling the negative component of prediction errors–reward omission and worse-than-expected outcomes 11, 12. The reward and outcome signals are delivered by excitatory glutamatergic and cholinergic inputs from the PPTg, lateral hypothalamus, ventral pallidum, and other structures, many of which are themselves partially mixed with expectation signals 14, 13. The individual dopamine neuron applies a common response function 15 to the net effect of these converging inputs, yielding a signed, quantitative error whose positive component (burst) or negative component (pause) is then broadcast to striatal and cortical targets via phasic dopamine release. Recent evidence that dopamine neurons exhibit stable heterogeneity in the relative scaling of positive versus negative error responses–consistent with distributional RL–adds the further nuance that even the subtraction itself may be asymmetrically parameterized across individual neurons, allowing the population to encode not just the mean error but a family of asymmetric errors spanning the return distribution 16, 3, 15. The upshot is that the RPE computation, though often written as a single subtraction, is biologically implemented as a distributed, multi-step, and redundantly organized process in which many brain areas partially pre-compute components of the error and the dopamine neuron refines this into a more complete signal 14, 2, 17. A 2024 computational study compares temporal representations (Figure) 19. The study implements a biophysically inspired model (Figure). The simulations track changing cue and reward responses (Figure).
